content.summary_of_the_paper: This work is concerned with a very practical scenario of Federated Learning where the participating clients may not have access to labelled data. It proposes a sophisticated approach where clients locally employ a combination of FixMatch and MixMatch to expand the datasets, followed by a convex combination of L_fix with additional data augmentation and a mixup loss L_mix to optimise the model parameters. Experiments are provided in supports of its operability and qualitative arguments are provided to differentiate with respect to other works.
content.main_review:
Strengths 
- Addresses an important aspect of FL
- Interesting combination of approaches to extend SSL from centralised to federated setting

Weaknesses
- Given the fairly involved approach, it is unclear how each part contributes to the overall effectiveness.
- Similarly, the effect of different hyperparameters can be investigated which currently have been adopted from their centralised counterparts.


Other comments
- Overall the approach was clear, the only drawback is its complexity makes it difficult to interpret the benefits of its different components. For example, what happens if strong augmentation is used at both client and server ends? Or if _lambda_ is set to zero and only L_fix is used for optimising? 
- I am also unclear on what is being referred to as “Parallel” and “Alternate” in Table 2. 
- I would also recommend the use of standard terms, for example, _active users_ wasn’t immediately obvious in the contributions and its definition is only mentioned later in the text.
content.summary_of_the_review: I think this work demonstrates interesting results for semi-supervised federated learning which are comparable to centralised case. However, as mentioned above a more systematic analysis of why particular design choices were made to devise this approach, and preferably with experimentation would certainly help improve the quality of this work.

content.title: Thank you for the time and comments. We address each comment below.
content.comment:
1. We have included ablation studies on hyperparameters such as $\beta$ and $\lambda$, and the results are shown in Tables 7 and 8 in the Appendix. We do not use strong augmentation on the server because we want to compare centralized FixMatch fairly since they only use weak augmentation on labeled data.

2. Here, 'Parallel' means a (standard FL) aggregation of model parameters from the server and clients who are updated in parallel in each round. 'Alternate' means we first aggregate client models into one and then update it (also called 'fine-tuning') using the labeled data at the server, which is then used for initializing the next round. Our major novelty is the alternate training between the labeled server and unlabeled clients. In the revision, we illustrate the difference between alternate training and naive combination of FL and SSL in Figure 1. We also added ablation studies for two components of alternative training, namely 'fine-tuning with labeled data' and 'pseudo-labeling with received model' in Table 2. The results show that alternate training, which means a combination of 'fine-tuning with labeled data' and 'pseudo-labeling with the received model,' significantly improves the baseline performance.

3. Following your suggestion, we now use the terms 'active clients' and 'active rate' and define them when they first appear in the revision.

replying_to: Replying to SemiFL: Communication Efficient Semi-Supervised Federated Learning with Unlabeled Clients
display_title: Official Review of Paper4197 by Reviewer Yyfe

content.summary_of_the_paper: Previous work related to federated learning (FL) is based on an unrealistic assumption: each client holds labeled data. On the contrary, this paper studied a more practical scenario in FL, that is, the semi-supervised federated learning (SSFL) scenario. To this end, the authors proposed a semi-supervised federated learning framework called SemiFL. In SemiFL, the client holds completely unlabeled data, while the server holds a small amount of labeled data. In particular, SemiFL integrates some mainstream communication efficiency and semi-supervised learning techniques well. Furthermore, the authors provide a theoretical understanding of semi-supervised learning (SSL) using strong data augmentation. Extensive case studies illustrate that SemiFL can outperform many existing FL results trained with fully supervised data and is competitive with the most advanced centralized SSL methods.
content.main_review:
The strengths and weaknesses of this paper are summarized as follows:
Strengths:
+ The problem studied in this paper is important and needs to be solved in SSFL
+ Good writing
+ Sufficient theoretical analysis
+ Interesting theoretical findings

Weaknesses:
- Need to include more related work that is highly important
- Need more justifications about the novelty claims 
- Need to add more experiments to show that the communication is efficient
- Need to add more benchmark datasets
- Need to add more hyperparameter experiments

Comments:
1.  The following important references are missing, e.g., [1][2]. Furthermore, the format of the references requires careful proofreading—for example, reference [3].

[1] Zhang Z, Yao Z, Yang Y, et al. Benchmarking semi-supervised federated learning[J]. arXiv preprint arXiv:2008.11364, 2020, 17.

[2] Long Z, Che L, Wang Y, et al. FedSemi: An Adaptive Federated Semi-Supervised Learning Framework[J]. arXiv preprint arXiv:2012.03292, 2020.

[3] Jeong W, Yoon J, Yang E, et al. Federated Semi-Supervised Learning with Inter-Client Consistency & Disjoint Learning[J]. Proc. of ICLR.

2.  In the Introduction Section, the authors merely emphasized the practicality of semi-supervised federated learning. However, the authors still need to provide more details on the difficult challenges of combining semi-supervised learning techniques with federated learning. The reason is that this will make readers feel that the authors are just naively combining the two techniques.
3.  The authors claimed that the proposed method is communication efficient, but there are no relevant comparative experiments to support these claims.
4.  In this paper, the authors seem to simply combine the current mainstream semi-supervised learning techniques with the existing batch norm techniques, which reduces the novelty of the paper. It would be better if the authors could provide more justifications to enhance the contribution claimed in this paper.
5.  The semi-supervised learning part in the paper is very close to [1][2]. Then readers may be curious about the difference between this paper and [1][2]. Therefore, the authors need to provide more details to enhance the difference between them.
6.  The Federated LEAF dataset is a standard benchmark for federated settings, so it would be better if the authors could add an NLP dataset (i.e., Federated Shakespeare dataset) to evaluate the proposed SSFL algorithm.
[4] Caldas S, Duddu S M K, Wu P, et al. Leaf: A benchmark for federated settings[J]. arXiv preprint arXiv:1812.01097, 2018.
7.  The number of communicated clients is a significant factor affecting SSFL performance. Therefore, it would be better if the authors could explore the performance of the proposed algorithm under the setting of the number of different communicated clients, like [1].
8.  Will the alternate training proposed in this paper generates additional computational or operational costs? It would be better if the author could add a more detailed analysis.
9.  In this paper, the amount of labeled data on the server significantly affects the performance of the proposed algorithm. Therefore, authors should explore the algorithm's performance under different supervised data ratios (that is, the ratio of supervised data to all data). In addition, the author should keep the proportion of supervised data consistent when comparing performance, especially when comparing fully supervised and centralized semi-supervised.
10. The editorial quality of this paper is not always satisfactory. It contains quite a lot of inconsistent/non-precise descriptions, as also reflected in the above comments.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper tackles a very interesting problem, and the many technical considerations, as well as the experiments on various datasets and comparisons with existing SSFL techniques, are commendable. Some issues (unclear communication efficient contribution,  naïve combination issues, and hyperparameter experiments) still prevent me from recommending complete acceptance. More clarifications are necessary, and by adding some more "realistic'' experiments, I believe the paper could be turned into a significant submission of ICLR. I recommend a "5'', but my score can be easily increased to 6 by addressing the many clarifications expressed in my review. Further experiments and the concrete use-case would further improve my score.

content.title: Thank you for the time and comments. We address each comment below.
content.comment:
1. In our first version, we compared our method with two existing works FedMatch and FedRGD, which are the citations [1][3] you mentioned. We note that there may be some misunderstandings about these two citations. [1] changed its title from ''Benchmarking semi-supervised federated learning'' to ''Improving Semi-supervised Federated Learning by Reducing the Gradient Diversity of Models'' (as shown on Arxiv). [2] changed its title from ''Federated Semi-Supervised Learning with Inter-Client Consistency'' to ''Federated Semi-Supervised Learning with Inter-Client Consistency \& Disjoint Learning.'' When they published in ICLR last year, they used the title without '\& Disjoint Learning' (You can find the previous version on Arxiv). We add '\& Disjoint Learning' to the reference of [3] in our paper and include [2] as related work.

2. In the revision, we highlighted that a significant novelty is the alternate training between labeled server and unlabeled clients.  In particular, we illustrate the difference between alternate training and naive combination of FL and SSL in the newly added Figure 1.

3. We use the word ''communication-efficient'' to emphasize that our experimental setting is similar to FedAvg (local training for multiple epochs to facilitate convergence) rather than FedSGD (batch-wise gradient update). We believe it is a convention in the FL literature.

4. We added ablation studies for two components of alternative training, namely 'fine-tuning' and 'labeling upon receiving' in Table 2. The results show that alternate training, the combination of 'fine tuning' and 'labeling upon receiving', significantly improves the baseline performance. FedMatch paper is also one of the baselines we compare in Table 3. We point out that previous works, including FedMatch and FedRGD, fail to outperform the bottom-line case, where one trains with only labeled data ('Partially Supervised'). To our best knowledge, our work is the first SSFL method that not only outperforms 'Partially Supervised' case but also performs close to the centralized and federated 'Fully Supervised' case. The current performance cannot be obtained without the joint consideration of alternate training, strong data augmentation, and sBN. Furthermore, we provide a theoretical understanding of the role of strong data augmentation used in SSL, the first in the literature to the best of our knowledge. 

5. The major difference between our work and [1][2] is alternate rather than parallel training. [1][2] adopt parallel aggregation of model parameters from the server and clients while our method updates the aggregated client model with labeled data at the server. The novelty of our work was also highlighted in our response to your point (c).

6. We did not use the LEAF dataset because we needed to compare our results with SSL methods, and not all the FL datasets were used for semi-supervised learning tasks. In particular, SSL methods like FixMatch used the CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and SVHN datasets. It is also not clear how we can combine strong data augmentation with NLP data. We need to point out that our experiments have used the most comprehensive benchmark datasets compared with [1][2][3].

7. In Table 3 of the revision, we have performed experiments with different active rate $C$ to adjust the number of communicated clients at each communication round.

8. The limitation of alternative training is that we need to update the aggregated client model with labeled data which will delay the computation time. We mentioned this in the revision.

9. In Table 1, we vary the 'Number of Supervised' and demonstrate the performance of the proposed algorithm under different supervised data ratios. We note that in Table 1, 'Fully Supervised' means all data are labeled while 'Partially Supervised' means only the 'Number of Supervised' data are labeled.

10. Following your comment, we have edited several descriptions in the revision to clarify our contribution and technical details. If you have further concrete suggestions, we will revise them accordingly.

replying_to: Replying to SemiFL: Communication Efficient Semi-Supervised Federated Learning with Unlabeled Clients
display_title: Official Review of Paper4197 by Reviewer v9ki

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors tackle Semi-Supervised Federated Learning, where clients have completely unlabeled data while the server has a small amount of labeled data, and propose a method called SemiFL, which performs strong augmentations on unlabeled data and trains the labeled server and the unlabeled clients alternatively. SemiFL is evaluated and compared with the existing SSL, FL, SSFL methods on several benchmark datasets.
content.main_review:
This paper is well-written and -structured. The motivation is interesting and the problem definition is clear.

For the methodology and evaluation parts, however, several critical points are required to be improved or addressed.  

- *Lack of Novelty*: SemiFL seems more like an application of a bunch of prior works to the semi-supervised federated learning scenario. For example, the proposed method consists of three components, (1) strong data augmentation, (2) alternate training, and (3) static Batch Normalization. For (1), I was not able to find novel contribution points from the proposed augmentation technique but realize it is a combination of the existing techniques of FixMatch, MixMatch, and Mixup. Similarly, for (3), adopting sBN is also hard to see their own significant contribution to the ML community. For (2), alternate training seems somehow novel, but still not significant. To the best of my knowledge, one of the prior works, FedMatch, studied disjoint learning with two sets of parameters for supervised and unsupervised learning, which shares a similar concept to the proposed SemiFL method.


- *Comparison of SemiFL and FL/SSFL methods*: the results seem strong, but the experimental setup is quite confusing. (1) Can you use the same network for other methods as well? The different choice of the base networks makes analyzing the results much harder. My suggestion is to simply use WResNet28x2 for all methods. (2) Can you use the same normalization technique for other methods? I personally think that adopting the sBN technique should be tone-down and the choice of normalization techniques should be identical across all methods for proper evaluation.


- *More Benchmark Datasets Required*: while the comparison with SSL methods uses three datasets (CIFAR10, 100, SVHN), only CIFAR-10 is used for the comparison with FL and SSFL methods. It is highly recommended to use at least two more datasets and show consistent results in order to support your arguments.
content.summary_of_the_review: As several critical enhancements are desired in terms of novelty and evaluations, I am unfortunately not able to recommend acceptance at this time.

content.title: Novelty concerns
content.comment: Thank the authors for their detailed responses. In fact, reviewers want to see more descriptions of your novel SFL method than just experimental results. However, alternate training is common in SFL. This is our big concern.

replying_to: Replying to Novelty concerns

content.title: About novelty
content.comment:
1) As we mentioned in 'To all reviewers', we describe our novel SSFL method in detail by adding an illustration in Figure 1, indicating two components of our method (``Fine-tuning with labeled data`` and ``Pseudo-labeling with received model``), and elaborating why these two components matter in Section 3.3. We also added ablation studies of each component, as demonstrated in Table 2. The results show that our novel method is the key to improving the performance of the labeled server and performing competitively with the state-of-the-art fully supervised FL and centralized SSL methods.  
2) We need to point out that we do not agree with the claim that ''alternative training'' is common in the SSFL literature. To our best knowledge, none of the previous SSFL works, such as those mentioned by Reviewer Yyfe in the first review, used ''alternative training''. In particular, FedRGD [1] aggregates local models and the server model from groups of clients in parallel, FedSiam [2] 'uses a siamese network to utilize the unlabeled data on each client', and FedMatch [3] 'separate the supervised and unsupervised learning via the decomposition of model parameters into two sets of parameters, one for supervised learning and another for unsupervised learning'. We believe our method is the first method that can actually improve the performance of the labeled server, and we hope future works can improve upon our result. Therefore, it is not fair to claim our method is not novel without any evidence.

Dear Authors,

Thank you very much for your detailed reply and hard work. I am sorry that this paper has not received positive reviews. Really Sorry. However, the reviewer responded as follows in response to the issues complained by the authors:

(1)  As the author, the reviewer had also submitted papers to top venues such as KDD, WWW, CIKM, and CCS. After that, the reviewer turned his attention to how to write a paper that could attract reviewers in a short period of time. Reviewers believe that this skill is very important in an increasingly competitive academic world. Our negative evaluation does not mean that this work is not good, it may be due to our misjudgment, perhaps the writing skills of the authors, and other reasons. We are very sorry to disappoint your Ph.D. students.

(2) Indeed, for me, this paper has the following issues: a) This work needs to be compared with other communication efficient FL schemes instead of FedAvg to support the claimed communication efficiency; b) Reviewers want to see the authors propose novel semi-supervised techniques that perfectly integrate with FL; c) As mentioned by the reviewer v9ki, the methods in this paper are a combination of some existing popular SSL techniques. In the revised version, the reviewer did not see the relevant additional experimental results to eliminate his concerns, so the reviewer reduced the score (from "5" to "3").

Review sincerely hopes that the authors, especially your Ph.D. students, still believe in the beauty of academics and continue to put a lot of effort into academics. replying_to: Replying to Response Letter

content.title: Thank you for response
content.comment:
(1) We thank the review for his detailed responses.and patient explanation. As a PhD student, I still have a lot to learn from the experienced researchers. I really appreciate your advice on attracting reviewers, but I do think the reviewers have the obligation to read the papers and discuss with the authors to clarify their concerns. The success of ICLR is closely related to its merit of open discussion and transparency. After all, I personally believe the ultimate goal of academia is to produce better works but not to compete for publishing in the top conference. I understand that each reviewer has his/her own unique view. We did address most of your concerns in the revision and response. 

(2) We address the issues you mentioned as follows. a) As we reply for your first comment, we use the term 'communication-efficient' mainly to emphasize our work is rooted from FedAvg rather than FedSGD. FedAvg has the merit of local training of multiple epochs to reduce communication cost and facilitate convergence. If we naively combine semi-supervised learning (SSL) methods with FedAvg, the extensive local training will diverge the model parameters of each local client and this is the critical reason that previous semi-supervised federated learning (SSFL) works fail to perform closely to the state-of-the-art federated learning (FL) method. Moreover, we did compare our work with other communication-efficient FL methods such as FedDyn and HeteroFL, and illustrate communication cost in Table 3. b) Our work focuses on demonstrating a straightforward but feasible combination of existing semi-supervised learning and FL methods, because previous works fail to outperform the ‘Partially Supervised’ case (training only with labeled data) where they cannot improve the performance of labeled server with unlabeled clients. We believe it is a fundamental issue that has not been addressed in the SSFL literature. We hope future works can utilize our works and better semi-supervised learning methods that possibly specialized for FL to outperform our strong baseline. c) We did conduct additional experiments to address the concerns of reviewer v9ki in the revision. As for the first concern of technical novelty, we conduct ablation study in Table 2 to demonstrate the effectiveness of each component of alternative training, and we also illustrate the idea of alternative training in Figure 1. Meanwhile, to address the second concern, we compare our results with existing SSFL works under the same experimental setup as illustrated in the small table in the response box for reviewer v9ki and in Table 3 in detail. Finally, we also compare our work with HeteroFL in Table 6 for more datasets to address the second and third concern of reviewer v9ki.

Our work focuses on demonstrating a straightforward but feasible combination of existing semi-supervised learning and FL methods, because previous works fail to outperform the ‘Partially Supervised’ case (training only with labeled data) where they cannot improve the performance of labeled server with unlabeled clients. We believe it is a fundamental issue that has not been addressed in the SSFL literature. We hope future works can utilize our works and better semi-supervised learning methods that possibly specialized for FL to outperform our strong baseline.

(2) We disagree we need to compare with SSFL methods on more datasets because existing works like FedMatch and FedRGD fail to outperform the ‘Partially Supervised’ case (training only with labeled data). Our result already performs closely to the state-of-the art FL and centralized SSL method. Moreover, FedMatch (ICLR2021) and FedRGD only publish their results on MNIST and CIFAR10. Our experiments are conducted on CIFAR10, CIFAR100 and SVHN under various FL settings including IID vs. Non-IID, different number of supervised data, normalization, and model architecture. Therefore, we believe we have solid evidence that our work outperforms existing works.

replying_to: Replying to Thank you for response

content.title: Response
content.comment: The claimed performance is better than all previous work does not mean that novelty is enough. Novelty is often related to the research problem itself. For example, what is the real problem in FL? In real life, are there any commercial companies deploying SSFL systems?

replying_to: Replying to Response

content.title: Thank you for response
content.comment: We never claim that better performance means novelty is enough. We point out that to our best knowledge, our method is the first work that can improve the performance of labeled server with unlabled clinets while previous works, although tackling similar problem, fail to do so. Both reviewer v9ki and Yyfe claim our approach "alternate training is common in SSFL". We believe the reviewers need to provide justification and evidence on why our method is not novel enough. The reviewer Yyfe said "Novelty is often related to the research problem itself". However, previous discussions are about technical novelties but not about the novelty of the problem of semi-supervised federated learning (SSFL) itself. We follow previous published works on this topic and produce better methods to solve the problem. We believe this is a common workflow in academia. Furthermore, "any commercial companies deploying SSFL systems" is not related to novelty but rather a practicability issue. First, FL is still an on-going research topic and many recent advancement of FL systems have not been deployed commercially. Second, SSFL is a relatively new topic and only appears in recent years. Therefore, it is too early to decide whether SSFL has commercial practicability or not.
